items.question: Why did you feel uneasy about discussing AI consciousness while working at DeepMind?
items.object: Discussing AI consciousness while working at DeepMind
items.answer: I joined DeepMind in 2017. At that point, I'd been thinking and writing quite a bit about consciousness. But then I sort of stopped because I didn't think it seemed appropriate for somebody working in a corporation to be talking about consciousness, especially in the context of AI, because it might sound like we're trying to build conscious AI, which I don't think is a good look or a particularly good project either.

items.question: Why do you think today's large language models make it increasingly difficult to avoid discussing consciousness?
items.object: Consciousness attribution to large language models
items.answer: The thing is, with today's generation of large language models, I think it's becoming increasingly difficult to avoid the subject because people, whether we like it or not, will ascribe consciousness to the things that they're interacting with. And we see this left, right and center. People, even people who know exactly how they work, say things like, “Well, I think large language models are a little bit conscious.” Ilya Sutskever said, and we had the Google engineer who ascribed consciousness to one of our models. And I think we're going to see this more and more and more. Whether or not I think it is the right term, whether it is appropriate to talk about them in terms of consciousness, it's going to happen anyway. So I think it's really important to actually think through these issues and think, well, what do we mean when we use the word consciousness, and how do we apply it to exotic cases? And this is really, really important: how might our language change to accommodate these exotic and strange things that have come into our lives?

items.question: What do you see as the danger of anthropomorphizing large language models?
items.object: Anthropomorphism of large language models
items.answer: The danger of anthropomorphism, I think, is in thinking that a system such as a large language model, a chatbot or something, has capabilities that it doesn't. It's as simple as that, actually. It's also thinking, perhaps, that it lacks capabilities that it does. So in both cases, I think we can go wrong. We can go wrong because they exhibit very human-like linguistic behavior. We can just assume that they are going to be very human-like in general, in all of the rest of the behavior that we encounter with them. We can find that at one moment a large language model might make a ridiculously stupid mistake that no child would make, and in the next moment it's saying something extraordinarily profound philosophically.

items.question: How has Janus's article “Simulators” influenced your way of thinking about large language models?
items.object: Janus's article “Simulators” and the role-play view of large language models
items.answer:
I was also very impressed and influenced by that article. So basically they are advocating a certain way of looking at large language models and their behavior. What they say is that we should think of a large language model as a kind of simulator, which is capable of simulating language-producing processes of various sorts. And it's capable of simulating all kinds of language-producing processes. In particular, it's capable of simulating people and humans, and it's capable of simulating different kinds of humans: humans who are playing different sorts of roles, who may be helpful assistants or humans who are crazy psychopaths.

Indeed, in their way of thinking of things, these are all examples of simulacra. Simulacra in their conception include actually not only human beings, but anything that produces language at all. So your base model can simulate anything that can generate language, if you like. Of particular interest, of course, are humans and human language producers. The particular class of simulacra that I'm interested in really are humans playing different roles. In the work that I've been doing, I've been thinking of language models in terms of role play and their ability to play a part, if you like. So this was very much inspired by and drew on the work of Janus.

items.question: Why do you regard the idea of a “superposition of simulacra” in Janus's article “Simulators” as important for understanding a language model's conversation?
items.object: The “superposition of simulacra” in Janus's article “Simulators”
items.answer:
I think they make another very, very interesting and important point in that article, which is that they draw attention to the fact that large language models, at any point in an ongoing conversation, produce the next word or string of words, the next sentence, as a product of a stochastic process. What the underlying language model generates is a distribution over the possible words that might come up next. Then you sample from this distribution to come up with an actual word. That's the word that you give back to the user. For example, if you asked the language model to tell you a story and it says, “Once upon a time, there was,” at that point, as at all the points up to that, it's going to generate a distribution of the possible tokens that might come next, possible words that might come next. It might say, “a beautiful princess,” or “a handsome prince,” or “a fierce dragon.” It could say any of those things depending upon the sampling process. You can rewind the conversation, come back to that point again, sample again, and get a different answer and take the whole story off in a completely different direction.

What they draw attention to is the fact that, at any particular point in a conversation, there's really a whole set of roles being played by the underlying simulation at any one point. The conversation shapes what role is being played. In that sense, it's unlike a human being because, as they put it, you've got a whole superposition of simulacra that are all being simulated all at once. As the conversation progresses, the actual distribution of simulacra is being narrowed down.

items.question: What do you think playing 20 Questions with a large language model reveals about its apparent commitment to an object?
items.object: A large language model playing the object setter in 20 Questions
items.answer:
You can play this with a large language model, of course. You can ask the large language model to play the part of the setter who thinks of the object, and then you play the part of the guesser who tries to guess the object by asking questions. If you do this with a person, if a person is not cheating, as it were, they will think of an object in their head, fix that object in their mind, and that's that. Then they'll answer the question according to what object they've thought of in advance.

A large language model can't really do that unless you use some hack or another. What it really does is, you say to it, “Think of an object,” and it says, “I've thought of an object.” It hasn't really thought of an object. It's just issued the tokens to say the words, to say that it has. But then you will ask a question and you'll say, “Is it larger than a house?” and it'll say, “No.” Eventually, if you say, “Oh, I give up, tell me what the object is,” then it will say, “Oh, I was thinking of a pencil,” and it will typically give you an object that's consistent with all of the answers it gave to all of your questions. But then if you just wind back one and resample and ask it again, “Okay, I give up, what were you thinking of?” it might say a mouse or a bottle, or it could say something completely different, which indicates that it had never really committed to any particular object in the first place.

In theory, you could rewind further and it might actually give you a different answer to the questions. That's because what you've really got is a whole tree of possibilities. This stochastic sampling process at any point in a conversation induces a whole tree of possibilities that branches forth from where you are right now. Counterfactually, you can always rewind the conversation to an earlier point and revisit it and sample again and go off on a different branch. My coauthors of that paper, the Nature paper, Larry Reynolds and Kyle MacDonald, have this system called Loom, which allows you to retain the whole tree of a conversation. You can visualize this, and revisit different points in the conversation and resample and explore the thing as a whole kind of tree of possibilities.

items.question: How do you interpret a large language model’s account of its own consciousness during pauses in a conversation?
items.object: A large language model’s account of its own consciousness during pauses in conversation
items.answer:
Of course, when we're interacting with a large language model, from the point of view of the underlying implementation, it's very stop-start. You issue some prompt or question or whatever to the large language model and then it produces its response. If you go away and make a cup of tea before you continue the conversation, then there's absolutely nothing going on inside that large language model or the instance that you're interacting with during this. It's totally dormant, just sitting there. Now, this is very different obviously to human consciousness, unless we're asleep; even if we're asleep, we're dreaming, and there's all kinds of stuff going on inside our heads. But consciousness is an ongoing, continuous process. If we stop this conversation briefly while I go to the loo or something, you're not going to just suddenly go all dormant and stop doing anything. Your brain is going to have all kinds of ongoing activities. So this is a very different sort of thing. So I said, “What happens to your consciousness during the pauses between our interactions?”

It had a really very good answer to this, which was along the lines of, “Well...” By the way, whenever these things use the term consciousness, I retain a great deal of skepticism about whether those terms are actually genuinely applicable. But what's interesting, the way I read their answers, is that they're articulating a conception of consciousness that might actually apply to something like this, even if it doesn't apply to this one before me right now.

So there's a very interesting philosophical exploration. It says things like, “Well, I think consciousness for me is actually very different from the kind of thing it is for a human being. And I think that during the pauses between our interactions, I no longer exist at all in any kind of meaningful sense.” It gave an answer along those lines, typical of many of the answers that it gave, which were along the lines of there's a very different kind of consciousness, kind of selfhood, kind of this, that or the other that is applicable to entities like me. But I can articulate it, and here it is. When I put it all that way, of course, I'm anthropomorphizing this thing quite a lot in the way I'm describing it right now. But just to go back to the role-play thing, as far as I'm concerned, it's playing a role. It's playing the role of a kind of philosopher talking about consciousness and so on. And it's doing a pretty good job, I would say.

items.question: How do you understand agency in today's large language models, including models that can use tools?
items.object: Agency in large language models
items.answer:
The term agent is used in all kinds of different ways in the AI literature. There's a very lightweight notion of agency, which is something that simply performs actions in some environment and gets some kind of sense or perceptual information back from the environment in a loop. That's how we can talk, for example, about a reinforcement learning agent. That concept of agency, of an agent, is very, very lightweight and doesn't carry much philosophical baggage. But as soon as we talk a bit more earnestly about agents and agency, then we bring on a lot more philosophical baggage. If we talk about something that is acting for itself, and that's what we mean by an agent, I think the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy article is alluding to something a bit more like that, and that's going a whole extra step. To my mind, in today's large language models, we don't see agency of that sort at all, really. The only actions that they can perform are issuing responses to the users.

Let's caveat that immediately, because people are introducing all kinds of extra functionality to these models, as new things are being announced on an almost daily basis. One thing we see is so-called tool use. Today's models can make external calls to APIs that can do all kinds of things, send emails, book hotel rooms for you, potentially all kinds of stuff. So that's greatly expanding the action space beyond just issuing text to the user. Those things are a bit more agent-like. Again, you have to be nuanced about the way you use the words, because there is a bit—it can act as an agent on your behalf. In that sense of the word, it's a bit more agent-like, but it's still not acting for itself. In that full-blown notion of agency that's alluded to in the Stanford Encyclopedia article, it's still not acting for itself. So we still don't have agency in that sense. That would be a whole extra step.

The causal microstructure is all about physical objects and the way they interact with each other, physical substances, liquids and gases and gravity and stuff like that. We acquire what I've called foundational common sense by interacting with the everyday physical world and the particular causal microstructure that it has.

items.question: How do you view the idea that understanding something like transitivity requires innate structure in the mind?
items.object: Innate cognitive structure and the understanding of transitivity
items.answer: In the case of something like transitivity, this is a classic argument in philosophy between the rationalists and the idealists, dating back to the 17th and 18th century. Kant supposedly resolved this by reconciling these two opposites. The Kantian argument would be that there's a certain amount of innate structure that has to be there in the mind to understand the world at all. Maybe when we think about that empirically, we may find that evolution has endowed us with certain basic templates for understanding the world. Maybe it's things like transitivity, something that's there in the same machinery that supports language. These are all empirical questions. I don't know what the latest research on all of these things is, but it does seem to me that that's a reasonable position to take.

items.question: How do you understand the distinction between treating a system as if it were conscious and its consciousness being a fact of the matter?
items.object: The distinction between treating a system as conscious and its consciousness being a fact of the matter
items.answer:
I'm a bit resistant to the distinction, to the very distinction. This is a very difficult position to maintain because we have a very, very strong intuition that there is a fact of the matter about our own consciousness, and it's very difficult to escape from that basic intuition. I have a whole approach to these kinds of questions. A question that really motivated me was: suppose that we come across some object which is a completely alien artifact, and maybe there's consciousness going on inside this artifact. This thing could be conscious, but we might never know. Suppose that it were a white cube deposited in front of your lab and you were tasked with the problem of whether it would be moral to throw it down a mine shaft and forget about it.

My approach to these problems is that in order for the question of whether something is conscious or not to be answerable or askable, we need to be able to engineer an encounter with the putatively conscious being. What I mean by that is that we have to be able to put ourselves in a position where we're sharing a world with that putatively conscious artifact or being. A good example is the octopus. Peter Godfrey-Smith has written these wonderful books about what it's like to hang out with octopuses and be with them. The really important aspect of that is that he has to put on a diving suit and go down and be under the water and spend time with the octopus, interacting with the same things and being in the same world together, seeing the same things. On that basis, and the behavior that he observes, he might come to start treating it as a fellow conscious creature.

By analogy, what I think we need to be able to do is to engineer an encounter like that, even if it's a very alien kind of artifact. Suppose it's this white cube. One way that it might happen: scientists may manage to figure out that there's computation going on inside this white cube, and then they manage to reverse-engineer this computation. They can see that there's a division between a world and things interacting with that world in this computation; there's a sort of simulated world. Then you could imagine, by some clever engineering tricks, inserting yourself into that very same world and being alongside these things that are interacting with this environment, and interacting with that environment with them. So, being in the world with them. Obviously, I'm setting this up to be very much like a game environment and a virtual world, but to make the thought experiment work. That's an example where, if you manage to engineer an encounter with these things that are inside this cube, you can observe their behavior, interact with them, and decide whether you may or may not start to treat them as fellow conscious creatures.

There are these two steps: can you engineer an encounter, at least in principle? That makes the question answerable. Then you can answer the question by actually having the encounter and interacting with them. By the way, we notice that everything there is public. There's no private realm of subjectivity here. It's on the basis of public stuff that you come to see them as fellow conscious creatures or not.

items.question: Why do you find Wittgenstein's private language argument such a powerful challenge to dualism about consciousness?
items.object: Wittgenstein's private language argument as a challenge to dualism
items.answer:
It's all about the idea that we have, or that we can talk about, private sensations, things that are purely subjective and that only I as an individual can understand and know what they mean. What red is for me, internally for me. The private language remarks undermine that very conception.

What he means by a private language is very important to get this right. He doesn't mean a language that I've invented and that nobody can understand just because I've invented it. The reason it's a private language is because it's about something which only I can access subjectively, which is what red is like for me. It's the idea that you can have a word for that completely internal thing that is just mine. He says, imagine that I keep a diary, and every time I have this particular experience, I write “S” in my diary to label that I've had that experience. Maybe I think I'm having this experience on a particular day and I write “S,” and a few days later I think I'm having that experience again, so I write “S” again. The question he asks is: what possible criterion could there be for the correctness of that word? What would make it actually stand for anything meaningful, given that what really makes words meaningful is if they're understandable in a public setting, if they're understandable to other people? There can be no criterion for correctness that anybody else could validate for this thing, insofar as it stands for something that's completely private.

There's a whole set of remarks that, after he sets up this little thought experiment, tell you the implications of it. There's one really key phrase where Wittgenstein is always engaging with an imaginary interlocutor, an imaginary person who's arguing with him in the book. He's imagining this person says, “Aren't you saying that the sensation itself is just a nothing? Aren't you a kind of behaviorist? You're just saying that it's a nothing.” His answer to this is, “Well, I'm not saying it's a nothing, and I'm not saying it's a something either. The point was only that a nothing would serve as well as a something about which nothing can be said.” That little paradoxical-sounding, weird-sounding statement encapsulates something really profound. When I first really understood what he was getting at there, it had a really dramatic shift in the way I thought about consciousness, subjectivity, and to my mind, it is the thing that really undermines dualism. It's the most powerful way to undermine the dualistic intuitions that we have and that date back to Descartes and before Descartes, but were articulated very well by Descartes.

items.question: What do you count as public evidence when discussing consciousness?

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between consciousness and cognitive abilities such as intelligence and creativity?
items.object: Consciousness and its relationship to cognitive abilities
items.answer:
When we're using the word consciousness, often we are using it in the context of certain behavior and behavioral inclinations, and we use it in the context of other humans and other animals. The word consciousness is a multifaceted concept, alluding to many things. One of the things it's alluding to is our ability to deal flexibly with the everyday world. We speak about, “Oh, I didn't notice the chair. That's why I bumped into it,” or, “I didn't see that there was a desk over there that might have had something interesting inside it if you opened it up.” We talk about our awareness of the world, and at the same time we're talking about an aspect of consciousness and a whole load of behavioral dispositions and capabilities. These things are very much related to each other in our everyday speech.

Then the question arises: are they dissociable? It's not like I think consciousness is some metaphysical thing whose essence is out there to be discovered. It's a concept that we invent and a word that we use to describe the world around us and our place in it and each other. The question is: are there things that we might create or imagine where we'd want to use one concept, one set of words, and not use the other? That's what the question comes down to. In the case of something like AlphaGo, we're all kind of agreed that there's a kind of cognition going on there, a kind of reasoning, certainly a lot of cleverness, a kind of intelligence, and even, if we're thinking about move 37, a kind of creativity. Sometimes in our usage we're going to bundle the things together, and sometimes we're not. This is all a practical matter of how we use language and how it's usefully deployed. It's not about discovering some metaphysical entity that's out there, which is what the word consciousness denotes.

items.question: How do you understand the usefulness of Daniel Dennett’s intentional stance when describing machines?
items.object: Daniel Dennett’s intentional stance
items.answer: I think you can use and deploy the concept of the intentional stance without necessarily embracing everything that Dan Dennett was talking about in that context. For him, there's a whole big philosophical position around it, but there's a very simple sense of the intentional stance that we can lift from Dan without necessarily buying into everything that he said. We often in everyday terms speak about artifacts and animals as if they were rational agents that act on the basis of what they believe and what they want. Whether they really do believe or have desires, it's useful for explaining and understanding their behavior. If we adopt the intentional stance towards a chess machine, a chess computer, a chess program, or a Go program, we might say, “It advanced its queen because it wants to try and pin down my rook.” This is just a natural way of speaking. If we use that way of speaking, it's good in every way, because we can discuss among ourselves what the machine is doing, explain what it's doing, and predict what it's going to do. That's taking the intentional stance, and it doesn't necessarily bring with it a belief that these concepts are literally applicable. Maybe they are or maybe they're not.

items.question: How do you think anthropomorphism can distort our understanding of contemporary AI's cognitive capabilities?
items.object: Anthropomorphism and the cognitive capabilities of contemporary AI
items.answer: In the context of contemporary artificial intelligence in particular, the danger of anthropomorphism, I think, is in thinking that a system such as a large language model, a chatbot or something, has capabilities that it doesn't. It's as simple as that, actually. It's also thinking perhaps that it lacks capabilities that it does. In both cases, I think we can go wrong. Because they exhibit very human-like linguistic behavior, we can just assume that they are going to be very human-like in general, in all the rest of the behavior that we encounter with them. But we often find that's not the case. At one moment, a large language model might make a ridiculously stupid mistake that no child would make, and in the next moment it's saying something extraordinarily profound philosophically, or summarizing some enormously difficult scientific article really accurately. These things have superhuman-ish capabilities, translating something into four different languages all at once. So it can be better than human in some directions, but clearly very deficient in others. Contemporary models can make all kinds of stupid mistakes, they can confabulate, they can make errors of reasoning and just say daft things. Those are examples of where it's a mistake, on the basis of a certain amount of interaction, to think, “Oh, it's just like a human,” because you can misjudge it in many ways.

items.question: How do you judge when it is appropriate to say that a current chatbot understands something?
items.object: Understanding and anthropomorphism in current chatbots
items.answer:
I'm not sure I'd go so far as to say they don't reason or they don't understand or they don't form beliefs. Rather, my approach is to say that we should be very cautious in using those terms. Those would all be examples of taking the intentional stance if we were to use those bits of terminology to describe what a current chatbot or conversational AI was doing. It's perfectly reasonable to do that in very many cases. I would never make the blanket claim, “They don't understand.” I think that's not quite right. Sometimes it's appropriate to say, “Oh yeah, it seems to understand very well what this big long article about nuclear physics was all about, and it summarized it really well. It really understood it.” Somebody might say it really did seem to understand it, and I wouldn't say they were wrong in using that phrase there.

But then on another occasion, you might find that it—for example, recently people have been posing this classic goat, cabbage, fox problem, where you've got a boat and you have to cross a river with a goat, and you can't have more than two things in the boat at once, and you can't have the goat with the cabbage and all this kind of stuff. It's a little puzzle, and you have to cross lots of times and do all kinds of trickery. People posed this to some large language models: “I've got a boat and a cabbage and I need to get the cabbage to the other side of the river. How do I do it?” Several of the models start to come up with this totally baroque solution that involves going backwards and forwards, and sometimes they invent goats that aren't even in there because they've overfit or connected with this classic problem. No child would make this stupid mistake. There you would say, “Well, obviously, it just didn't understand.” It's quite right to say “didn't understand” in that case. The anthropomorphism comes about when you think that it understands when we understand and doesn't understand when we don't understand. The reality is that sometimes it will understand when we understand and sometimes it won't. It's all mixed up. The mistake is to think that it is like us.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for improving large language models' ability to reason?
items.object: Improving reasoning in large language models
items.answer: In the case of reasoning, clearly today's large language models do struggle very often with reasoning problems. This is an open research problem, and people are making a lot of progress in improving their ability to solve reasoning problems. The right approach is an open research question. Maybe you throw more training data at it that includes lots of reasoning problems, and eventually you get sufficient generalization there. It's not totally clear that that will work, but maybe it will. Maybe you include external calls, say to a planner or some kind of external reasoning system, and incorporate that, make something that's kind of a hybrid that uses that more symbolic approach. Or, in my work with Tony Cresswell at DeepMind, we introduced this selection-inference framework, where you treat the large language model as a module that does bits of reasoning, and you have a surrounding algorithm that makes calls to the module in a sequence of reasoning steps. So you have an outer algorithm. There are lots of ways of trying to tackle that problem. But take your basic large language model today as it is at the moment and put it in a chat interface, and it's easy to find reasoning problems that are going to stump it.

items.question: How do you assess today's large language models' ability to solve abductive reasoning problems?

items.answer: Abductive problems are where we are looking for an explanation for something. You'll find a large collection of abduction problems that you could just present to today's large language models, and they would do quite well at them. At the same time, I'm sure it wouldn't be too difficult to find problems, especially if they involve many steps, where it will go wrong. The multiple steps are where today's large language models are a bit weak. It's an open research question; people are working on all that. If there are multiple steps and step N is dependent on step N minus one, they're inherently very computational sorts of things in that sense. Large language models are a bit weak at that for sure. We can introduce things like chain of thought to try to improve that, but they're of limited success. My feeling is that those are not the things where large language models themselves are inherently strong, and you should probably make use of other tools to boost reasoning capabilities, like the ones I listed. Sometimes that means making external calls to dedicated reasoning components. Sometimes it's embedded in the large language model, in a reasoning algorithm itself. You can go either way: take the large language model and put reasoning things inside it, so it makes external calls, or do it the other way around. You can have a reasoning algorithm and make the large language model a component of the reasoning algorithm.

items.question: How do you assess the Turing test as a measure of intelligence?
items.object: The Turing test as a measure of intelligence
items.answer: I think it's a pretty rubbish measure of intelligence. items.question: Why do you think the test of consciousness in Ex Machina, which you call the Garland test, is such a good test?

Caleb says, “Oh, what you're doing is you're trying to build something that passes the Turing test.” Nathan says, “Oh no, we're way past that. items.question: How do you judge whether today's large language models fulfill the spirit of the Turing test?
items.object: Today's large language models and the spirit of the Turing test
items.answer: It's very tricky territory. Again, I think we should distinguish consciousness and intelligence in this regard, although there are relations between the two, or consciousness and cognition. What I wanted to say about the Turing test is I do feel that today's large language models kind of pass the spirit of the Turing test. We defined the Turing test earlier, the popular conception, and as I remarked, you can kind of game it and there are certain problems with it. items.question: How do you distinguish Turing’s original Imitation Game from the version of the Turing test used in contemporary academic discussion?
items.object: Turing’s original Imitation Game and the contemporary Turing test
items.answer: What I meant by the popular conception—I think maybe “popular conception” isn't quite right—is the sort of contemporary version of it that's used in academic discussion. There is a human adjudicator there, but the difference is that Turing sets up the test with some specificities about the number of minutes you spend interacting with it. He also sets it up in the context of this party game where the aim is to try and work out which you've got, a man and a woman, that somebody is conversing with via paper, and they don't know which is the man and which is the woman. They have to guess which is which. That's the way the thing is set up in the original paper, by analogy with that. There are all kinds of peculiarities in the original paper, if you're a Turing scholar, that aren't really relevant to the contemporary way that we think of the Turing test.

items.question: In what sense do you think today’s AI systems pass the spirit of the Turing test?
items.object: Today's AI systems passing the spirit of the Turing test
items.answer: I also think that the sense in which today's systems pass the spirit of the Turing test is only the spirit of the Turing test because, of course, you very often can immediately tell that it's an AI, not least because it'll just tell you right away. If you ask it, it'll say, “Well, as a large language model trained by Google or OpenAI...” So it's easy to tell which is which. items.question: How do you interpret the argument in Thomas Nagel’s paper “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?”?
items.object: Thomas Nagel’s paper “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?”
items.answer: The point of this paper was to draw attention to the fact, if it is a fact, that there are creatures very different from ourselves, from humans, but that we assume have some kind of consciousness. In his terminology, we assume that it's like something to be that creature. He chose a bat because bats are very obviously very different from ourselves. They fly, they use sonar. They're pretty weird animals. The thinking is that, well, it's probably like something to be a bat, but what it's like is going to be very different from what it's like to be a human. Nagel uses that example to get at a whole metaphysical idea, which again I would say is pointing to a kind of dualism, to suggest that there's a whole realm of facts about subjectivity which are outside of the purview of objective science but which nevertheless are part of reality. For him, I feel it alludes to a sort of dualistic way of thinking, that there's this realm of facts about subjective things and a realm of facts about objective things.

items.question: How do you see physicalism and idealism as ways of avoiding mind–matter dualism?
items.object: Physicalism and idealism as ways of avoiding mind–matter dualism
items.answer:
I guess a physicalist thinks that there is only one substance in reality, and that's material reality, there is no separate stuff of mind metaphysically. For the physicalist, there is no dualism if they really think that. But the trouble is that as soon as you probe, often they struggle to deal with dualistic intuitions about subjectivity.

The idealist, on the other hand, also thinks that there's only one substance, but that substance is the substance of mind. Physical reality has to be a kind of construct out of this one substance, out of mind stuff. So that's a very different way of avoiding dualism. But it has its own problems about how do you account for science and the success of science and so on.

items.question: Why do you find the panpsychist view that every physical object has some consciousness so counterintuitive?
items.object: Panpsychism and its application of consciousness to physical objects
items.answer:
I guess for the panpsychist, insofar as I understand these philosophical positions—I shouldn't put myself forward as somebody who necessarily understands them in depth. Everybody who subscribes to these views has a slightly different version of them as well. The panpsychist certainly thinks that reality is composed of physical material substance, but that physical material substance irreducibly has a psychological dimension to it, a mental dimension to it. Every physical object has a little bit of consciousness in it, if you like, in some sense.

I find it a very difficult view to articulate because I find it so completely counterintuitive. I can't really put the panpsychist hat on and express their point of view. You need a panpsychist here to do that. With my Wittgensteinian hat on, I think, “How do we use words like consciousness?” We use the word consciousness and all the related terms in the context of each other, of other human beings, in the context of our being together in the world, and you're behaving in certain ways and we're exchanging certain looks when we're doing things, and we understand each other as fellow conscious creatures. That's the context in which we use words like conscious. When I speak about, “You're not conscious, you're asleep,” it's all in the context of other humans that we use those words. It's ludicrously inapplicable to use that word in the context of a brick or a toaster or an atom. The words simply are not applicable in those contexts.

items.question: How do you think philosophical puzzles about consciousness should be approached?
items.object: Wittgenstein’s approach to philosophical puzzles about consciousness
items.answer: Personally, I think all of these positions involve a great deal of mental gymnastics, and I reject any kind of -ism. What I mean by that is I don't use that term to describe my views at all. All of these -isms are misguided. What we need to do is dismantle the whole way of talking which makes us confused in the context of these kinds of issues. That's what Wittgenstein is trying to do, to, as he puts it, show the fly the way out of the bottle. There's this famous phrase. The fly is the person who's ended up thinking all these philosophical thoughts by taking ordinary language into strange places, taking it on holiday. To show the fly the way out of the bottle is to bring all of these concepts back to their ordinary everyday usage and to show thereby that you haven't really lost anything. The puzzles evaporate. So that isn't an -ism. That's a critical methodology for shifting the way that you think and talk altogether.
